vignette:
He is a 62-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life in operating rooms, moving with the steady, exacting rhythm of a surgeon. Before the accident, he describes himself as disciplined and efficient, someone who trusted preparation, repetition, and control. He has been married for many years, and he and his wife built a life around long hospital hours, early mornings, and the quiet confidence that comes from doing work that demands precision. He does not talk about himself much; he talks instead about duty, about patients, about keeping his hands steady.

The accident happens on an ordinary day, which is part of what makes it difficult for him to understand even now. He is driving home after a long shift when another vehicle crosses into his lane. He remembers the sudden brightness of headlights, the violent impact, and then a moment in which everything feels suspended and unreal. The car spins. Metal crushes. Glass explodes across the interior. He knows, with the detached clarity that sometimes comes in moments of danger, that he may die there. His body is trapped. He can smell gasoline and dust, hear his own breathing becoming shallow and fast, and feel a panic he later describes as unlike anything he has known in the hospital. He has spent decades responding to other people’s emergencies, but in that moment he is powerless, waiting for strangers to reach him.

In the early weeks afterward, he moves through recovery with the same stubbornness he brings to surgery, but inside he feels altered and brittle. He returns home physically injured and shaken, and at first he tells himself he should be grateful to be alive. He says this often, as if saying it enough might make it true. Yet sleep becomes fragmented. He wakes abruptly in the night with his heart pounding, certain for a few seconds that he is trapped again in the wrecked car. He does not want to burden his wife with the details, so he turns away from her in bed and lies rigid in the dark, listening to the house. During the day, he notices that his mind goes back to the crash without warning: the screech of tires in traffic, the flash of sunlight on another car’s windshield, even the metallic smell of a busy garage can pull him back into the sensation of being crushed and helpless.

He begins avoiding driving whenever he can, making excuses to have his wife accompany him or asking others to handle errands. He chooses routes that feel safer, though “safe” is not really the word he uses; what he means is that he tries to reduce the chance of being startled. He is wary of intersections, impatient drivers, and loud unexpected sounds. At work, he remains outwardly composed, but he notices that his body is tense in ways it was not before. When an ambulance siren passes the hospital or when an operating room alarm sounds sharply, he feels his chest tighten and his muscles brace before he has time to think. He keeps working because work is what he knows, yet he no longer experiences the same ease with it. He double-checks things more than before, and if something interrupts the flow of a procedure, he becomes more irritable than he would have admitted in the past.

He also finds himself less patient at home. His wife says he seems “far away,” and he recognizes the truth of it. He sits in the living room but feels cut off from the room around him, as though part of him stays back at the crash site. He has trouble finding pleasure in the things he once enjoyed, including long dinners with family and weekend gatherings. He is not openly tearful, but he feels a flatness that unsettles him more than sadness would. He thinks often about mortality in a way that is not philosophical but immediate, almost intrusive. The accident has shaken his belief that careful people stay protected. He knows that many of his patients live with uncertainty, yet he now feels the vulnerability in his own body. Sometimes he catches himself imagining another collision when he is on the road, and he grips the steering wheel hard enough that his knuckles pale.

Even now, months later, he speaks about the accident with a controlled voice, but his body tells a different story. When he recalls it, his breathing changes and his gaze drops. He remains a man who takes his obligations seriously, who still shows up for work and family, but he is carrying the crash with him in a way that interrupts sleep, sharpens fear, and makes ordinary life feel suddenly less dependable than it once did.
